body.objective: Students will be able to analyze a scene as a director.
body.iCan: I can analyze a scene as a director.
successCriteria: I can find the meaning and turning point of a scene
I can make blocking and pacing choices that support meaning
I can give clear, respectful notes to actors
body.hook: Actors look at a scene and ask "What does my character want?" A director looks at the same scene and asks "What is this whole scene about, and how will the audience feel it?" Directing means seeing the big picture.

vocabulary.definition: The person responsible for the overall vision and staging of a production.
The director's overall interpretation of the play.
The moment in a scene where things change.
How actors are arranged on stage to create a picture.
The speed and rhythm of a scene.
Feedback a director gives an actor after a rehearsal.

study.title: Seeing Like a Director
study.question: How does a director shape a scene's meaning for the audience?
study.passage:
Use a short two-person scene (for example the kitchen scene from the previous lesson or a teacher-chosen scene).
Step 1, The spine (10 minutes): In one sentence, what is the scene about underneath? ("A daughter protects her father from news that could change the family.")
Step 2, Turning point (5 minutes): Mark the moment where the relationship or situation shifts.
Step 3, Stage pictures (15 minutes): Plan three tableaux: opening, turning point and final image. Use levels (sitting, standing), distance (close or far) and focus (where the audience looks) to show the relationship.
Step 4, Pace map (5 minutes): Mark where the scene should speed up, slow down or hold a silence.
Step 5, Direct (20 minutes): Rehearse with two actors. Give notes using the sandwich method only if helpful, but always be specific and actionable: "On 'More hours,' take a beat and look at the letter's hiding place before you speak."
Note-giving rules: speak to the character's action, not the actor's personality; one or two notes at a time; ask questions ("What does Maya want here?").
study.source: Original directing activity written for this lesson.
discussion: How did distance between actors show their relationship?
Where did a silence work better than a line?
What made a note useful or unhelpful?

study.product: Direct a peer scene: submit the spine, three sketched stage pictures, a pace map and your rehearsal notes, then present the scene with a one-minute director's introduction.

examples.title: Spine
examples.problem: Write a spine for a breakup scene.
examples.answer: "Two people realize they've been holding on out of fear of being alone"
examples.explore: How would this change the blocking?

examples.title: Distance
examples.problem: How can blocking show two characters growing apart?
examples.answer: Start close, then increase distance each beat

examples.title: Pace
examples.answer: At the turning point, to let the audience feel it
examples.explore: What happens if everything is slow?

examples.title: Note
examples.answer: "On your last line, try to stop him from leaving with your voice, not your body"

practice.q: Name three tools for stage pictures.

practice.a: The character higher up often seems more powerful.

practice.q: Why give one or two notes at a time?
practice.a: Actors can absorb and apply a few clear changes.
It tells the actor something specific to do.

practice.q: Why plan the final image of a scene?
practice.a: It is the last thing the audience remembers.

practice.q: How can silence be a directing choice?
practice.a: A held pause can create tension or let a moment land.

practice.q: Why direct notes toward the character's action, not the actor?
practice.a: It keeps feedback respectful and playable.

practice.q: How can two directors stage the same scene differently?
practice.a: Different spines lead to different blocking, pace and focus.

practice.q: How should a director handle an actor who disagrees with a note?
practice.a: Listen, ask questions and find a choice that serves the scene.

misconceptions: Thinking directing means telling actors exactly how to say lines
Thinking every scene should move quickly
exitTicket: Write a spine for a scene you know.
Rewrite "Be angrier" as a playable note.

items.q: The director is responsible for
options: A) the overall vision and staging
items.answer: A) the overall vision and staging

items.q: A turning point is
options: C) the end of the play
items.answer: D) where the scene changes

items.q: Pace refers to
options: B) the speed and rhythm of a scene
items.answer: B) the speed and rhythm of a scene

items.q: A note is
items.answer: B) feedback for an actor

items.q: A scene's spine is
options: B) what it is about underneath, in one sentence
C) the backbone of the set
items.answer: B) what it is about underneath, in one sentence

items.q: Which shows a relationship growing apart?
items.answer: D) increasing distance between actors

items.q: Which is an actionable note?
options: C) On that line, try to stop her from leaving.
items.answer: C) On that line, try to stop her from leaving.

items.q: The character on a higher level often appears
items.answer: D) more powerful

items.q: Why plan a final stage picture?
options: B) It is the last image the audience remembers
D) It is required by law
items.answer: B) It is the last image the audience remembers

items.q: A director slows the pace at the turning point to
options: A) let the moment land with the audience
items.answer: A) let the moment land with the audience

items.q: Notes should focus on
items.answer: D) the character's action

items.q: Two directors staging one scene differently is
items.answer: A) normal because interpretations differ

items.q: Define director.
items.answer: The person responsible for the overall vision and staging.

items.q: What is pace?
items.answer: The speed and rhythm of a scene.

items.q: Write a spine for a scene you have studied.
items.answer: Answers vary.

items.q: Explain how distance can show a relationship.
items.answer: Closeness suggests intimacy or conflict; distance suggests separation.

items.q: Give one rule for giving notes.
items.answer: Be specific, speak to the action, one or two at a time.

items.q: Why plan three stage pictures?
items.answer: They show the opening, turning point and final image clearly.

items.q: Explain how a director's vision shapes blocking and pace.
items.answer: The spine decides where actors move, when pace changes and what the audience focuses on.

items.q: Rewrite a vague note into a specific, playable one.
items.answer: Answers vary.
